source.filename: 2023-A Single-Variable Zigzag Approach to Model Imperfect Interfaces in Layered Beams.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Layers are composed of the same homogeneous, linearly elastic, and orthotropic material with principal material axes aligned with geometric axes.
Small displacements, rotations, and strains are assumed.
Plane strain conditions prevail parallel to the x2-x3 plane.
Transverse normal stresses are assumed to be negligible compared to other stress components and set to zero (sigma_33 = 0) in the kinematic equilibrium formulation.

Interfaces between adjacent layers are treated as continuous zero-thickness mathematical surfaces where relative sliding is permitted but relative transverse normal separation or penetration is forbidden.
Interfacial sliding displacements and interfacial shear tractions follow a linear constitutive relationship governed by tangential stiffness coefficients.
Residual stresses from manufacturing and thermal stresses from environmental gradients are neglected.
control_variables: Beam length L and thickness h with length-to-thickness aspect ratio L/h = 5
Uniform layer thickness (t = h/n for n = 2 and n = 3)
Lamina orthotropic elastic properties: EL, ET = EL/25, GLT = EL/50, GTT = EL/125, and Poisson's ratios nuLT = nuTT = 0.25
Simply supported boundary conditions at x2 = 0 and x2 = L
Zero transverse normal displacement jump at layer interfaces
dependent_variables: Global kinematic variables: longitudinal displacement v02, transverse displacement w0, and rotation phi2
Local layer transverse shear stresses (k)sigma23 computed a posteriori from local equilibrium
Interfacial displacement jumps and shear tractions across adjacent layers
Stress and moment resultants N22, Q22, M22, and MZS22

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A homogenized zigzag theory enables modeling multi-layered beams with imperfect sliding interfaces as equivalent single layers, reducing degrees of freedom compared to layerwise discrete theories.

Decoupling the three displacement unknowns of the zigzag model into a single sixth-order ordinary differential equation in a fictitious bending variable circumvents shear-locking issues in numerical discretization schemes.

Decreasing interfacial tangential stiffness increases layer compliance, creating pronounced jumps in longitudinal displacements and bending stresses and increasing overall displacement magnitudes relative to perfectly bonded configurations.

As interfacial tangential stiffness increases to sufficiently high thresholds (K_S*h/ET = 10 for two-layer beams and 5 for three-layer beams), mechanical response converges asymptotically to that of perfectly bonded beams.

In three-layer beams with asymmetric interfacial stiffnesses, stresses and displacement jumps redistribute toward the more compliant interface, while interfacial shear tractions concentrate at the stiffer interface.

future_work: Extending the single-variable formulation to layered systems possessing elastic mismatch between adjacent layers.
Implementing the single-variable model into numerical isogeometric collocation schemes.
Incorporating modeling of thick interlayers or transition zones between adjacent layers as weak layers.
Accounting for thermal loads, residual stresses, and misfit strains.
independent_variables: Longitudinal coordinate x2 and through-thickness coordinate x3
Nondimensional interfacial tangential stiffness parameters (K_S*h/ET, K1_S*h/ET, K2_S*h/ET)
Number of layers and stacking sequence (two-layer 0/0 and three-layer 0/0/0)
Transverse mechanical loading distribution (sinusoidal versus uniform load)
limitations_inferred: The formulation was benchmarked only against simply supported boundary conditions; other boundary configurations (e.g., clamped or free ends) were not evaluated.
The study is entirely analytical and benchmarked against 2D elasticity exact solutions; no physical experiments on actual physical specimens were conducted.
Analyses were confined to static mechanical loading; dynamic, vibratory, and time-dependent degradation behaviors were not addressed.
The model is strictly a one-dimensional beam formulation under plane strain and was not demonstrated on two-dimensional plates or three-dimensional continuum geometries.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The formulation is restricted to beams with layers made of the same homogeneous material, excluding the effect of elastic mismatch between layers.
Interfaces are treated as sharp zero-thickness surfaces with zero relative transverse displacement, neglecting physical transition zones or finite-thickness interlayers.
Assumptions are limited to small displacements, rotations, and strains.
Transverse normal stresses are neglected in formulating beam kinematics and equilibrium (sigma_33 = 0).
Residual manufacturing stresses and thermal gradient stresses are not incorporated in the presented beam equations.
The approximate zigzag kinematics assume piecewise linear longitudinal displacement through the thickness, unable to match the nonlinear intra-layer displacement profile of 2D elasticity.
main_results: The coupled system of three differential equations for layered beams with imperfect interfaces was decoupled into a single sixth-order differential equation in a fictitious bending displacement variable.

Closed-form analytical solutions for simply supported two- and three-layer beams under uniform and sinusoidal transverse loads demonstrated strong agreement with Pagano's 2D exact elasticity solutions.
Interfacial compliance significantly amplified local displacements and bending stresses while creating distinct interfacial displacement jumps.
Increasing interfacial stiffness caused the structural response to transition smoothly toward the perfectly bonded limit, nearly overlapping at K_S*h/ET = 10 for two layers and 5 for three layers.

Interfacial stiffness asymmetry in three-layer systems led to significant redistribution of stresses and displacements, shifting jumps to the compliant interface and tractions to the stiffer interface.
The transverse loading pattern (sinusoidal vs. uniform) played a secondary role compared to the interfacial compliance in determining local stress and displacement profiles.
modeling_methods: Global first-order shear deformation kinematics enriched with local piecewise functions for interfacial displacement jumps.
Principle of Virtual Work for deriving homogenized equilibrium equations.
Decomposition of transverse displacement into bending and shear components to select a fictitious bending primal variable.
Sixth-order ordinary differential equation governing the fictitious bending displacement.
A posteriori evaluation of transverse shear and normal stresses through 2D local Cauchy equilibrium equations.
Comparison and validation against Pagano's 2D elasticity exact solutions via the transfer matrix method.
performance_metrics: Nondimensional local transverse shear stress (k)sigma23 determined from local equilibrium.
Degree of correlation/overlap with 2D exact elasticity solutions.
possible_gap_implications: The single-variable zigzag formulation for sliding interfaces could provide a computationally efficient, shear-locking-free framework for modeling variable-stiffness structures (e.g., layer-jamming mechanisms or friction-controlled laminated continuum structures) without increasing degrees of freedom as layer count increases.

The present model's restriction to identical layer materials, zero-thickness interfaces without transverse separation, and small-strain linear kinematics requires extension before it can model soft robotic systems involving large deflections, compliant elastomer matrices, or hyperelastic materials.
paper.research_objective: To develop and verify an accurate and efficient single-variable zigzag formulation for beams composed of homogeneous layers of identical material with imperfect, sliding-compliant interfaces subjected to transverse mechanical loading.
paper.research_problem: Layered structures with imperfect, compliant bonds or delaminations exhibit complex local stress and displacement distributions that govern stiffness degradation and failure; standard multi-variable and discrete-layer structural theories are computationally demanding or prone to numerical issues such as shear locking in finite element implementations.
stiffness_mechanism: sliding between layers at imperfect interfaces
paper.title: A Single-Variable Zigzag Approach to Model Imperfect Interfaces in Layered Beams
